messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 62
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Bank Teller
  trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another
  pcl5: 58

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Known People: Related people, Stress: Stress, Tactile (Unexpected Touch): Being touched unprepared
  Threat: Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert, Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard
  Memory: Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time, Guilt on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense guilt, Sudden Pieces: Fragments of the memory appear suddenly without warning and then disappear
  Negative Appraisals: Inadequacy: I am inadequate, Permanent Damage: I have permanently changed for the worse, Bad Coper: My reactions since the event show that I am a lousy coper

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Threat
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Triggers

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Martin Keller was 62 when he came for treatment, a soft-spoken white man who had worked as a bank teller for decades and who now described himself as “not the same person anymore.” The event he returned to again and again had happened a year earlier in an ordinary setting that still felt unforgivably close to daily life. Leaving the bank after a long, tense Friday, he had been hurrying through a crowded sidewalk near the entrance, distracted and keyed up from work. As he turned abruptly, he collided hard with an older customer he knew by sight from the branch, knocking her off balance. She fell backward, struck the pavement, and sustained serious injuries. Martin remembered the sound of her head hitting the ground, the startled faces gathering around them, and the awful instant of recognizing her as someone he had greeted many times across the counter. What lodged most deeply was that he had caused it. Since then, people he recognizes from the bank, especially customers connected in his mind to that day, have carried a charge that feels out of proportion even to him.

In the weeks afterward, Martin became convinced that the accident revealed something damning about him. He had come to believe he was inadequate, that a decent and competent man would not have moved so carelessly, and that the way he had unraveled afterward proved he was, in his words, “a lousy coper.” He also spoke as if the incident had marked him permanently: not just that he had made a terrible mistake, but that he had changed for the worse. Those conclusions were stirred most sharply by encounters that might once have been routine. If a familiar customer stepped up to his window, or if he saw a relative of the injured woman in town, he would feel an immediate drop in his stomach and think, there you are, the man who hurts people. On especially stressful days at the bank, when the line lengthened and coworkers called questions across the counter, he became harsher with himself, taking his tension as proof that he was fundamentally not up to ordinary life anymore.

Those same beliefs also made the memory harder to keep in the past. When Martin thought of himself as damaged and inadequate, the accident did not come back as a settled recollection but as something jagged and morally charged. Remembering it brought the same terror he had felt on the sidewalk, along with an intense wave of guilt that seemed to confirm his worst conclusions about himself. He did not describe a single orderly replay. Instead, fragments arrived suddenly and without warning: the woman’s shoes leaving the pavement, the crack of impact, someone shouting for help. In those moments it felt to him as if his mind were producing evidence against him.

The memory, in turn, seemed to keep his body organized around danger. Nights became especially difficult. Martin said he could not fall asleep because some part of him felt he needed to stay alert, as though letting go would be irresponsible. Even in his own living room beside his wife, he found he could not fully relax, despite knowing rationally that he was safe. He scanned rooms, watched doorways, and startled himself by tracking other people’s movements. When fragments of the accident broke through, the surge of terror left him superalert and on guard for hours.

That ongoing state of watchfulness fed back into the way the accident returned. Because he was constantly keyed up, stress at work was no longer just unpleasant; it became a condition in which pieces of the event seemed more likely to burst in. A rushed afternoon at the bank, the press of customers he knew, even sitting tense in bed listening for small household sounds could be enough for a fragment of the sidewalk scene to flash up and disappear again. He had begun to dread sleep not only because he could not settle, but because the quiet gave the memory room to appear.

His vigilance also widened the range of what felt dangerous. Martin had become acutely sensitive to unexpected touch. If a customer brushed his sleeve while handing over a deposit slip, or a coworker touched his shoulder from behind, he reacted as if jolted, instantly bracing and scanning the room. The more on guard he stayed, the more easily ordinary stress and contact registered as threats, and familiar people at work came to feel loaded before they had even spoken. In this way his own alertness seemed to prepare the ground for the next trigger.

By the time he sought help, his world had narrowed around the branch, his home, and the effort to keep himself composed in both places. His wife had noticed that he sat rigid in the evenings and no longer tolerated even casual touch unless he saw it coming. At work he was still showing up, but familiar customers now filled him with dread because they pulled him back into the conviction that he was a man who had done irreversible harm and had never recovered properly from it. He finally came in after a stressful day at the bank when a known customer approached his window, a coworker touched him unexpectedly from behind, and he felt the memory break over him in terrified fragments. What frightened him most was not only that this could keep happening, but that it meant his view of himself was true—that he had permanently become someone weak, unsafe, and beyond repair.
